passages.title: Should we bring back lost species?
passages.text:
[A] Across Europe, animals that disappeared centuries ago are returning. Beavers once again build dams in rivers where they were hunted out of existence, wild bison graze in forests from which they vanished long ago, and white-tailed eagles circle above coasts that had not seen them for generations. This process, often called rewilding, involves reintroducing species to areas they once occupied and then allowing natural processes to shape the landscape. Supporters see it as a way to repair damaged ecosystems. Critics fear that it creates new problems for the people who now live and work in those places.

[B] The beaver offers the clearest example of what rewilding can achieve. By building dams, beavers slow the flow of water through a river system, creating ponds and wetlands. These hold back water during heavy rain, which can reduce flooding downstream, and release it slowly during dry periods. In one fictional valley studied over ten years, the number of species of insects and amphibians around beaver ponds more than doubled. In my view, few engineering projects could deliver so many benefits so cheaply.

[C] However, the same dams can flood farmland, block drainage ditches and damage trees that landowners value. Farmers in several regions have complained that they were not properly consulted before beavers were released, and some have been angered by the loss of productive fields. These concerns should not be dismissed as simple opposition to nature. When farmers bear the costs of a project while the benefits are shared by society as a whole, it is understandable that they feel unfairly treated.

[D] Predators raise even stronger feelings. Proposals to return wolves or lynx to areas where they have been absent for centuries are frequently opposed by sheep farmers, who fear losing animals. Supporters of predator reintroduction point to evidence that predators can control populations of deer, which, when left unchecked, eat young trees and prevent forests from regenerating. The evidence for this effect is real but mixed: it appears strongest in large, wild areas and much weaker in landscapes that are divided by roads, farms and villages.

[E] There is also a question of what rewilding is trying to restore. Landscapes have changed enormously over the centuries, and the climate is changing again. A species that thrived in a particular valley five hundred years ago may not find the same conditions there today. Some scientists therefore argue that the aim should not be to recreate the past, but to build ecosystems that can cope with the conditions of the future. I find this argument persuasive, although it makes the goals of rewilding projects harder to define and to measure.

[F] Money is an important factor. Reintroducing a species is expensive: animals must be captured, checked for disease, transported and monitored for years. Several projects have failed because funding ended before populations were large enough to survive alone. On the other hand, rewilded areas can attract tourists, and in some rural communities wildlife-watching holidays now provide more jobs than traditional farming. It would be wrong, however, to assume that this will be true everywhere.

[G] The most successful projects appear to share certain features. They begin with long discussions with local residents, they offer compensation or practical help to landowners who suffer losses, and they reintroduce species gradually so that problems can be identified early. Projects that were announced suddenly by national organisations, without local support, have tended to face lasting opposition, even when the scientific case was strong.

[H] Rewilding is sometimes presented as a simple choice between nature and people. That framing is, I believe, misleading. The real question is how the benefits and costs of returning wildlife can be shared fairly. Where that question is answered honestly, there is every reason to expect that more lost species will find their way home.

coach.message: Bài “Conservation: summary completion”: Điền từ nguyên văn theo giới hạn từ và trật tự ngữ pháp. Trước khi thử, hãy nói một việc bạn sẽ kiểm tra ở bài này.

Bạn đang xem “absorb rainwater” (verb phrase), nghĩa là “hấp thụ nước mưa”. Ví dụ: “Marsh soil can absorb rainwater after storms.”. Hãy tạo một câu mới liên quan đến conservation: summary completion thay vì chép lại.

Ở ví dụ có hướng dẫn “Complete with NO MORE THAN TWO WORDS: A marsh can slow the flow of ____ into streets.”, hãy làm bước này trước: Check the printed word limit and the grammatical slot separately. Chỉ mở mẫu sau khi tự thử.
Lỗi dễ gặp ở bài “Conservation: summary completion”: Không điền “heavy storms” vì thứ chảy vào phố là nước. Trích đúng “water” từ đoạn; 1 từ và phù hợp ngữ pháp sau “of”.

Bạn đã hoàn thành bài “Conservation: summary completion”. Hãy đánh dấu bằng chứng trong văn bản; lưu cụm “absorb rainwater” nếu thực sự muốn dùng lại, rồi sửa một chỗ chưa chắc chắn trước khi làm bài mới.
Bài này mình luyện Summary Completion về bảo tồn tự nhiên. Hãy đọc đoạn rồi tìm phần nào trả lời đúng câu hỏi; chưa cần đoán ngay.
Bạn đang bị bẫy: storms: là nguyên nhân thời tiết, không phải hiệu ứng giảm. Hãy đọc bằng chứng “reduce flooding further downstream” rồi thử lại.
Hãy phân biệt: water: xuất hiện ở câu trước nhưng không phải thứ chạm tới cây mới. Bằng chứng cần đối chiếu là “allowing sunlight to reach new plants”.
Bạn đã tìm đúng cả hai bằng chứng. Hãy vào phần luyện độc lập; Coach sẽ không tự chen vào.
